articles.title: Fantasy Football Panic Meter, Week 4: Which Year 2 RBs are we most worried about?
articles.summary: Ray Garvin goes over players he's worried about going into Week 4 for fantasy football.
articles.body:
Three weeks into the fantasy season, the excuses start getting a little harder to make. One bad game? Fine. Two games? We can still talk ourselves into patience. By Week 4, though, we have enough information to start asking whether what we drafted is actually what we have.

For running backs, I care about more than just touches. Seventeen carries can look great in a box score, but what kind of carries are they? Is the player involved on third down? Is he catching passes? Is he getting the football near the goal line? Is the offense creating enough scoring opportunities?

That is where this week's Panic Meter starts.

The thresholds remain the same: No Panic, Some Panic, Total Panic or Coping Corner. All four of these Year 2 running backs have disappointed in some way. They just haven't disappointed for the same reasons.

The carries keep pulling me back in with Omarion Hampton. Almost everything else is pushing his ceiling away.

Through three games, Hampton has 50 carries for 193 yards and two touchdowns. That is enough volume to keep him playable. The problem lies in the kind of work he is getting.

Hampton caught 32 passes in only nine games as a rookie. Through three games this season, he has two catches on three targets. Alec Ingold caught three passes for 35 yards in Week 3 alone. Hampton has fewer receptions through three weeks than his fullback had in one game.

Week 3 made the concern worse. Hampton played just 27 of 64 snaps and ran six routes. Keaton Mitchell played 23 snaps and ran 15 routes while Kimani Vidal handled much of the obvious passing-down work. Hampton saw only one of seven running back targets.

The Chargers are starting to split this backfield into three jobs. Hampton is the primary early-down runner, Mitchell gives them speed and Vidal is taking valuable passing-down snaps. That strips away the receiving ceiling fantasy managers were counting on.

The offense is not helping either. Los Angeles is 0-3 and has scored 14, 14 and 16 points, respectively. Even a secure goal-line role only goes so far when the team rarely gets there.

I'm at Some Panic. Hampton is still averaging more than 17 touches per game and has handled 50 of the Chargers' 68 running back carries, so the floor is still there. What has changed is the ceiling.

Fantasy managers drafted a three-down breakout and right now, all they have is an early-down volume back.

Ashton Jeanty represents almost the opposite problem.

The role is excellent. He has 76 touches through three games, 63 carries and 16 targets, and he played 83% of the snaps in Week 3. If you showed me that workload in August, I would have loved it.

Jeanty has 206 rushing yards on 63 carries — just 3.3 yards per attempt — with no rushing touchdowns. After opening with 102 yards on 23 carries, he has 104 rushing yards on 40 carries over the last two weeks. He also dropped three passes in Week 2 and failed on two early goal-line carries.

What has stood out most is the lack of the tackle-breaking and explosive rushing we saw from him as a rookie.

Mike Washington Jr. gave us a sharp contrast in Week 3. Jeanty's longest run on 19 carries was 12 yards. Washington turned five carries into 54 yards, including a 36-yard touchdown.

I'm not worried about Washington stealing the backfield. He played only 17% of the snaps. I'm worried because Jeanty is getting everything we want from a workload perspective and still has not consistently looked like the player fantasy managers paid for.

Las Vegas is 3-0 and averaging 29.3 points per game. The offense is creating scoring chances. Jeanty has two receiving touchdowns and still averages 18.4 PPR points, but the 32.7-point opener is carrying a lot of that number. Since then, he has scored 10.3 and 12.3, respectively.

So I'm staying at Some Panic. The workload is too strong to increase the panic level, but I need the explosive plays and tackle-breaking to return before I'm comfortable viewing Jeanty as the elite difference-maker fantasy managers drafted.

Quinshon Judkins has not been good. He also has not given me a reason to change the evaluation.

Through three games, Judkins has 42 carries for 124 yards, nine receptions for 53 yards and no touchdowns. He is averaging 3.0 yards per carry. Nobody drafted him expecting efficiency to carry his fantasy value.

His value comes from owning Cleveland's rushing work, and that part remains intact.

Judkins handled 18 of the Browns' 19 running back carries in Week 3 and finished with 70 rushing yards. Raheim Sanders took some passing-down work while Cleveland was chasing points late, but Sanders has only four carries all season. Jaleel McLaughlin barely played and Dylan Sampson is on injured reserve.

The setup is pretty straightforward. Judkins controls the early-down rushing work in an offense averaging 18 points per game. The receiving ceiling is limited and touchdown opportunities are going to determine a lot of his better fantasy weeks.

That doesn't mean I love the profile. It means the usage still matches the reason you drafted him. He is a volume-based RB2 or flex who can give you 15 to 20 touches and needs touchdowns to push beyond that. Three games have not changed the player or the role enough for me to react.

TreVeyon Henderson is the one I am most concerned about. He missed Week 1 with an ankle injury, returned in Week 2 and immediately gave fantasy managers hope with 16 carries for 76 yards and a touchdown.

Henderson played 21 snaps to Rhamondre Stevenson's 32. Henderson had a narrow 9-8 edge in carries, but Stevenson led 3-1 in targets and handled more of the passing-down work. Across Henderson's two active games, he has 25 touches to Stevenson's 18, but Henderson has only one target.

So yes, Henderson can lead this backfield in carries and still lose the snaps that carry more fantasy value.

Now, put that role inside a Patriots offense averaging 12 points per game. New England has scored 36 points in three weeks, the offensive line is dealing with injuries and Drake Maye has struggled to keep the offense on schedule. Henderson is being asked to create fantasy value without a reliable receiving role or control of the backfield.

We know he can create explosive plays. He averaged 5.1 yards per carry as a rookie, rushed for 911 yards and scored four touchdowns of at least 50 yards.

The problem is how much he needs those plays right now.

You cannot build a weekly fantasy expectation around waiting for a 40-yard run. That is Total Panic for me. The talent is still there, but the role is not strong enough and the offense is not producing enough points to cover for it.

Henderson can still save your week with one play, but New England is giving him very little else.

articles.title: Forsling's OT blast lifts Panthers past reigning Stanley Cup champion Hurricanes 1-0
articles.summary: Gustav Forsling hammered a shot past Brandon Bussi with 4.3 seconds left in overtime to lift the Florida Panthers past the reigning Stanley Cup champion Caro...
articles.body:
RALEIGH, N.C. (AP) — Gustav Forsling hammered a shot past Brandon Bussi with 4.3 seconds left in overtime to lift the Florida Panthers past the reigning Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes 1-0 in Tuesday's season opener for both teams.

On a night when the defenses and goaltenders had the edge, it was a blue-liner who provided the winning play to end a matchup of the last two teams to win the Cup.

The Panthers had their final chance with the game seemingly headed to a shootout as Carter Verhaeghe brought the puck into the zone with under 10 seconds left. But Verhaeghe sent the puck back toward Forsling, who fired a one-timer from near the blue line that zipped past Bussi's glove side to end it.

That spoiled the end of a three-month celebration for the Hurricanes since beating Vegas in June to cap a 16-3 march to the franchise's second Cup. The final piece was the players gathering at the blue line and tapping their sticks as a championship banner rose to the rafters.

That moment came against the Panthers, who reached the Stanley Cup Final for three straight years and won it all in 2024 and 2025. They had twice eliminated the Hurricanes in the Eastern Conference Final in their run, though injuries derailed last year.

Getting captain Aleksander Barkov back from that lengthy injury list was one of several reasons to expect the Panthers to jump right back into contention, along with Panthers star Matthew Tkachuk welcoming brother Brady as an offseason addition . There was also the change by bringing in Jacob Markstrom to take over the crease anchored by Sergei Bobrovsky during those title runs.

And for much of this one, it was up to Markstrom and Bussi to hold up in net, including against multiple one-on-one quality chances and a combined 13 power plays in regulation.

Markstrom finished with 15 saves while Bussi — who posted a shutout in Carolina's Cup-clinching win against Vegas — made 19 saves before giving up the last blast.

Panthers: Florida heads west to face the San Jose Sharks on Thursday.

Hurricanes: Carolina hosts the Washington Capitals on Friday night.

articles.title: Serena Williams’ new business move puts the next trillion-dollar company in focus
articles.summary: Serena Williams is no longer treating business as a side project.
articles.body: Serena Williams is no longer treating business as a side project. The tennis legend has turned her investment operation into a serious force in venture capital, recently rebranding Serena Ventures as Starfire Ventures. The firm now has 16 unicorns in its portfolio, while Williams says its ambition extends far beyond the next billion-dollar company. Her focus is finding overlooked founders, backing businesses with major potential and building a firm that can outlast her own name. At the same time, Williams is balancing investing with motherhood and a selective return to professional tennis.Serena Williams explains Starfire Ventures’ new directionThe rebrand from Serena Ventures to Starfire Ventures marks a deliberate change in how Williams sees the business. She said the original name worked, but she wanted the firm to become something larger than its founder.“We’ve just rebranded ourselves. . . . I felt like Serena Ventures is great, but I wanted it to be bigger than me. There are so many amazing people on the team, and there’s so much that we do. I felt like when you put a name on something, it can limit what you do. I want it to live on. I want this to be something that people look at years and years from now . . .”Williams says her approach to investing is driven mostly by a clear philosophy, with instinct also playing a role. Her firm has backed 16 companies that have reached unicorn status, giving the former world No. 1 a growing track record outside sport.She also pushes back against the idea that investing in women and underrepresented founders is simply a social exercise.“We invest in everyone. We invest in people who look like you. We invest in people who look like me. It’s just that we do see a lot of women and a lot of underrepresented founders because they know that we’ll hear their story. And we don’t invest in all of them. . . . We are only investing in winners. If we don’t feel the company is going to return our fund, we’re not going to invest in them. That’s just how we look at it.”Serena Williams is thinking beyond billion-dollar businessesWilliams sees an investment gap as an opportunity. She believes some founders are overlooked because investors do not always recognise their potential early enough.Her long-term goal is clear. “We’re thinking about the next billion-dollar company, the next trillion-dollar company, and how to be on those cap tables as well.”That ambition sits alongside a very structured personal life. Williams said she spends about 90% of her professional time with Starfire Ventures when she is not focused on her children.Her return to tennis is also carefully managed. Rather than pursuing another Grand Slam run, she has chosen a limited schedule that fits around her family and business commitments.“I’m not going back out there to win Grand Slams. I have a full-time job. But this is what I’m willing to do, and this is how I’m willing to show up.”For Williams, the next phase is not about choosing between tennis, business and family. It is about setting firm boundaries and deciding exactly where her time matters most.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: From days without food to CWG gold: Ashmita Dey now faces India's 32-year judo wait at Asian Games
articles.summary: Ashmita Dey arrives at the Asian Games less than two months after becoming the first Indian judoka to win Commonwealth Games gold.
articles.body: Ashmita Dey arrives at the Asian Games less than two months after becoming the first Indian judoka to win Commonwealth Games gold.The Commonwealth title in Birmingham changed her profile almost overnight, and the 24-year-old, who had spent much of her career out of the spotlight, began to be recognised off the mat too.“No one knew me before. But now everyone knows me. When I went to get food, someone said, this is the same girl, right? This is the same girl who created history for Judo for the first time in India. I was very happy to hear all this,” Ashmita told Timesofindia.comThe recognition means so much to her for a reason. Asmita’s career has been built through a combination of sporting support and financial uncertainty, with the latter shaping much of what she wanted from judo.Before the Commonwealth gold, there had been the bronze at the Asian Junior Championships in 2022, gold at the Junior Asia Cup in Macau in 2023, a silver at the Asian Open in Kuwait later that year, and another podium finish at the African Open in Casablanca in 2025. She had also finished fifth at the Asian Senior Championships in Almaty in April this year.The success and recognition have come a long way from a humble start in Belonia, a small town in Tripura, where her introduction to judo was almost accidental.Her uncle heard about trials at a sports school where there was running, jumping and a fitness test. Asmita had initially been around athletics trials, but judo became the sport that stayed.“My aunt thought I was talented and she put me in Judo and I started from there,” Asmita remembered.Within a week of starting judo, she competed in a jiu-jitsu event and finished first. Two or three weeks later came a state competition, where she won gold.The early years were sustained by family members moving her between places for training. Her brothers ferried her on a cycle for training, while her father would often travel with her from the village on a scooter, sometimes even in the rain.“My father used to support me a lot. He never stopped me for a game. My mother never stopped me.”When food was a struggle, a house became the dreamHowever, there were limits to what the family could provide. Asmita remembers periods when there was no food at home.“Because sometimes we didn't even have food. We used to sleep after drinking water. Sometimes we only had rice, salt, and chillies with water. Sometimes we used to get food once, sometimes twice. So I remember all those days.”Her mother had one gold earring, the only piece of jewellery she owned, and that was pawned for money. Asmita said she still has not been able to get it back, and the interest has continued to accumulate.Asked if she would get it back now, Asmita’s answer was immediate.“Yes, it will definitely come back. I have to get it.”Her father worked as a bicycle mechanic, taking whatever work he could find as the family struggled to make ends meet. The family lived in rented accommodation for years. Asmita grew up with the idea that a house of their own would have to come from what she could achieve.She had won her first competitions soon after starting, and her coaches were already telling her she could go further.By 2018, she had won silver at the Khelo India Games and moved to the Sports Authority of India Regional Centre in Bhopal. That was when she came under coach Yashpal Solanki - former Indian judoka and an Arjuna Awardee - after earlier support from Manik Lal Deb in Tripura.Solanki also pushed her towards international competition. “My coach used to say that I have to play internationally. I have to win a gold medal. He told me that I have to win a gold medal and have done that”Father's death, Commonwealth gold and what followedThe path, most recently, was interrupted by injury and, more painfully, by the death of her father. When she was injured in Delhi, he had travelled to her with her medicines.“When I was injured for the first time in Delhi, my father came to me. He brought all the medicines for me,” remembered Asmita.His death, in 2025, came with a Commonwealth Games trial coming up, and her coach called her back to training around the 12th or 13th day.There was about a month left.“I told him that I can't do it. I don't want to do it.”The coach then spoke to her about the Bhagavad Gita and death.“He told me that this is the truth. He used to read the Gita. I also read the Gita. He told me that this is the truth. One day, a person has to go. He motivated me a lot.”She returned to training. “To manage myself, I thought that if I cry and get weak, who will take care of my family? How will I make my house? I controlled my emotions a lot. You have to control your emotions a lot.”And before the final, there was only one thought. “I was thinking that I have to win and I have to get the gold medal.”She did, and the gold brought another reminder of the person she had lost. “Yes, I remembered my father a lot. If my father was alive, he would have been very happy. It was such a big achievement for me. He would have been very happy. I know that.”But there was another moment on the Commonwealth podium that stayed with her: the Indian flag and the national anthem, with athletes from other countries standing around her.“That was the biggest thing. I felt very proud.”Ashmita joined the Uttar Pradesh Police in 2023 through the sports quota. She was subsequently promoted to sub-inspector and, after her Commonwealth Games gold, was elevated to deputy superintendent of police (DSP). The job had already given her a measure of financial security and helped her take care of herself and her family.“I was so worried that I did so much in between. I have faced so much financially, but now I don't have to think much about that; I can [train with a] free mind. Now I can do better. I will do better.”The house, though, remains on her mind.“I always wanted to build a house. I had to do something. I had to do something big. Only if I do this, I can build a house. I always used to think like this. Finally, I can build a house now.”A tough Asian Games testNow comes the Asian Games, where Asmita will face a field led by several of Asia's established names in the women's -48kg category.Mongolia's Narantsetseg Ganbaatar is the highest-ranked entrant at No. 13 in the world, followed by Kazakhstan's Abiba Abuzhakynova at No. 19. Japan's Mitsuki Kondo, Uzbekistan's Laziza Haydarova, Hong Kong China's Ka Lee Wong and South Korea's Su Jin Jung are also in the 11-judoka field.There is another number that puts India's task in perspective. Judo has produced only five Asian Games medals for India, all of them bronze. Four came at the sport's debut at the 1986 Seoul Games, while Poonam Chopra won the fifth in the women's 56kg category at Hiroshima in 1994.India has not been on the Asian Games judo podium since. Indian judokas, by comparison, have won 15 Commonwealth Games medals.Asmita is entering a field led by higher-ranked Asian judokas, while carrying an Indian judo record that has not produced an Asian Games medal for 32 years.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Joga Purty breaks own national record again, storms into Asian Games quarterfinals
articles.summary: Kolkata: Joga Purty continued her rapid rise in Indian sport climbing by storming into the women’s speed climbing quarterfinals at the Asian Games on
articles.body: Kolkata: Joga Purty continued her rapid rise in Indian sport climbing by storming into the women’s speed climbing quarterfinals at the Asian Games on Tuesday while rewriting the national record yet again.The 19-year-old from Jamshedpur clocked 7.28 seconds in the qualification round at Portmesse Nagoya Exhibition Hall to finish ninth among Asia’s best speed climbers and secure a place in the knockout stage. In the process, she improved on her own national record of 7.37 seconds, a mark that had earned her a place in India’s Asian Games squad.Asian Games Full Coverage | Schedule | Medal TallyThe performance came as little surprise to those who have watched the teenager’s journey from close quarters.“Even when she first came to us in 2019, I felt there was something special about her,” said Babulal Rawat, her coach at the Tata Steel Adventure Foundation (TSAF) Climbing Academy. “Around 40 children had come for a trial, but the way she moved on the wall stood out immediately. She was climbing better than many athletes who had already been training for two or three years.”Purty’s road to the Asian Games has been far from smooth. Coming from a modest background in Jamshedpur, she was initially shy and often reluctant to compete. Today, however, she is among Asia’s top speed climbers.“There are very few female climbers in India who can match Joga’s level and pace during training. As a result, she often trains and races against boys,” said Rawat, a former climber who moved from Uttarakhand to Jamshedpur in 2014 and took up coaching in 2018. “That pushes her to compete harder every day and gives her an additional source of motivation.”The coach also stressed that international exposure would be critical if Purty has to fulfil her long-term potential.“When she goes abroad and trains against stronger climbers, that motivation becomes even greater, which is why international exposure is so important for her development,” he added.Purty’s 7.28-second effort, while a national record, also highlighted the gap that Indian climbers are trying to bridge at the highest level. China’s Lijuan Deng topped the qualification round with an Asian Games record of 6.23 seconds, while South Korea’s Jimin Jeong was second with a best time of 6.25 seconds.Rawat believes closing that gap will require sustained investment in the sport.“Sport climbing is still very new in India. Many people are not even aware of the sport. Athletes need regular international exposure and opportunities to compete against the world’s best. A short training trip abroad is not enough. If our climbers are to challenge for medals consistently, they need to compete internationally much more often,” he said.For now, though, his focus is on the knockout rounds of the Asian Games, where climbers race head-to-head on the 15-metre wall. Rawat believes Purty can lower the national record even further in Wednesday’s quarterfinal.“I still feel she can do even better. She has the talent to improve on her personal best,” he said.And judging by Tuesday’s performance, Purty has already shown she belongs among Asia’s elite, with the teenager from Jamshedpur continuing to push the boundaries of Indian sport climbing one national record at a time.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Vithya ran, Nithya prayed: The twin bond behind India’s new 400m hurdles record
articles.summary: Chennai: Far away from Aichi-Nagoya, at a gym in Chennai, Nithya Ramraj was too scared to watch Monday’s women’s 400m hurdles at the Asian Games live.
articles.body: Chennai: Far away from Aichi-Nagoya, at a gym in Chennai, Nithya Ramraj was too scared to watch Monday’s women’s 400m hurdles at the Asian Games live. She had her eyes tightly shut, either in prayer, pure fear or both.It was only when Nithya’s friends at the gym informed her that Vithya Ramraj had shattered the national record and won bronze that her twin sister opened her eyes.Asian Games Full Coverage | Schedule | Medal TallyVithya dedicated breaking PT Usha’s 42-year-old record to the person who had been rooting for her all along. For the Ramraj twins, moments like these are never individual ones to celebrate. Over the years, they have been each other’s strength, offering support and a helping hand whenever needed.Nithya, a 100m hurdler, was in the Chennai gym and not in Aichi-Nagoya because she is recovering from an ankle injury.“We knew she would break the national record, but we were waiting to see when it would happen. Vithya always calls me before and after she finishes a race. I just tell her to focus on the race and that we will be rewarded for the hard work. After I came to know that I would miss the Asian Games, she told me not to worry and said, ‘I will do double of what you would have done had you been part of the Asian Games.’ That is why she dedicated the medal to me,” Nithya told TOI on Tuesday.Their support for each other has found tangible measure. In 2021, after Nithya secured a job at Income Tax, she supported Vithya financially. Last year, the roles were reversed as Vithya stepped in to take care of Nithya and the family’s needs.Once Vithya equalled Usha’s record in 2023, there were always questions about when she would break it.“I have seen her struggles closely over the past three years, and that is why I was confident she would break the national record. I tell her that God has given her wings, and I ask her to lend them to me so that I can also run as fast as her. Unlike me, she is a very dedicated athlete,” said Nithya.While Vithya and Nithya chase their dreams on the track, their mother quietly misses having her daughters around.“It has been almost a year since Vithya last came home. Once we get married, we cannot spend as much time with our parents, and with the tight training schedule, we hardly get to go home now,” said Nithya.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Gulveer Singh completes Asian Games medal treble after gruelling five-day athletics test
articles.summary: Nagoya: Before leaving for training or competitions, Gulveer Singh has a ritual he never skips.
articles.body: Nagoya: Before leaving for training or competitions, Gulveer Singh has a ritual he never skips. He prays to a small statue of Lord Hanuman that he carries with him everywhere and applies vermilion to his forehead.By the time he completed his 5000m race on Tuesday night, the red mark between his brows had long been washed away by rain and sweat. But the 29-year-old had left an indelible mark on the Asian Games, completing a treble of medals: a bronze in the 5000m to go with silvers in the 10,000m and 1500m.Asian Games Full Coverage | Schedule | Medal TallyHis week at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium has been defined by perseverance, discipline and versatility. Built on a staple diet of daal, roti, sabzi, paneer and protein supplements, his lean frame has carried him through three gruelling races in five days, producing a feat rarely seen in Indian athletics.Gulveer clocked a personal best of 13:32.75 to finish behind Bahrain’s Birhanu Balew (13:30.79) and Japan’s Tomonori Yamaguchi (13:31.43).The three-medal haul, he said, was the result of sticking religiously to his routines and his coach’s plans.“I set out with the target of wanting to win three medals and I’m happy to have achieved that. I just listen to what the coach tells me and follow his plans. I never say, ‘Today I won’t do this.’ I follow the coach completely,” Gulveer said.Meanwhile, 3000m steeplechaser Avinash Sable, who finished fourth in his pet event, did not start.Pooja jumps to bronzeFor a while, Pooja’s name at the top of the high-jump leaderboard offered the possibility of a golden leap. The 19-year-old, however, had to settle for bronze after clearing 1.84m.The national record holder was flawless through 1.70m, 1.75m, 1.80m and 1.84m, clearing each height on her first attempt. She then failed all three attempts at 1.87m, but her clean card at 1.84m was enough to earn her the final podium spot on countback.Bronze in mixed relayHarita Bhadra, a last-minute inclusion in the squad, justified her selection by anchoring India to bronze in the mixed 4x100m relay.The quartet of Gurindervir Singh, Sneha Satyanarayana, Animesh Kujur and Harita timed a season-best 41.06 seconds.India were fourth heading into the final leg, but Harita, who won bronze in the 200m earlier in the Games, produced a strong finish to overtake Sri Lanka’s Shanthi Perera and bring India another bronze.China won gold in 40.78 seconds, while Thailand took silver in 40.87.India signed off their athletics campaign with one gold, nine silver and 14 bronze.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Gold again! India beat China and match world record in  Asian Games final
articles.summary: India retained the women’s compound archery gold medal at the Asian Games on Wednesday, producing a dominant performance against China and matching the
articles.body: India retained the women’s compound archery gold medal at the Asian Games on Wednesday, producing a dominant performance against China and matching the world record score in the process.The Indian trio of Jyothi Surekha Vennam, Chikitha Taniparthi and Prithika Pradeep defeated China 238-234 in the gold medal match at Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park to claim the top spot on the podium.Asian Games Full Coverage | Schedule | Medal TallyIndia equalled Korea’s world record score with the victory.China, represented by Wunier, Yue Wang and Fangyao Wei, had to settle for silver.The Indian team had earlier edged South Korea 234-233 in the semifinal to book its place in the title clash. The Korean trio of Park Jungyoon, Park Yerin and Kang Yeonseo went on to beat Chinese Taipei in the bronze medal match.The gold also meant India successfully defended the women’s compound team title won at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou.The semifinal against South Korea was closely fought from the start.India opened with 29 in the first three shots of End 1, with Chikitha and Jyothi hitting 10s while Prithika scored 9. South Korea, however, began with a perfect 30.The Indian trio responded immediately with a perfect 30 in the second half of End 1. South Korea’s Yerin Park scored a 9, leaving the two teams level at 59-59 at the end of the opening end.India eventually held its nerve to edge Korea 234-233 and advance to the final.The result capped another strong Asian Games campaign for India’s archers. At Hangzhou 2023, India enjoyed its most successful archery campaign at the Games, winning a record nine medals, including five gold, two silver and two bronze.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘We were still confident’: Dragan Mihailovic reveals belief behind India’s stunning Qatar comeback
articles.summary: Bengaluru: India men's volleyball coach Dragan Mihailovic said the team was confident of staging a comeback while trailing 0-2 and staring at a
articles.body: Bengaluru: India men's volleyball coach Dragan Mihailovic said the team was confident of staging a comeback while trailing 0-2 and staring at a straight-sets defeat against World No. 21 Qatar in an Asian Games Pool C match on Tuesday at the Park Arena Komaki in Komaki, Japan.The Serbian coach, credited for transforming the team which saw them win a bronze in the AVC Cup in Ahmedabad, said the team believed they could iron out the flaws and push hard. "Even after Qatar took a 2-0 lead, we were still confident that we were going to win this game because Qatar took the lead due to our mistakes. We knew exactly where we went wrong but it was almost impossible to fix it during those two sets because a few of our players were having a bad day," Mihailovic told TOI from Japan."We realized our mistakes in counterattack. Also, figuring out how to block against this excellent, young and talented player, Mubarak from Qatar, was the biggest problem for us until the last moment. He was the biggest problem for us until the last moment. "And I must say that this is a future star in the world of volleyball," the Serbian, also an FIVB instructor, said.Asked about India not consolidating their lead in the fifth set, Mihailovic said the Indian players lack international experience. "Unfortunately, our players have a significant lack of international experience. It's completely different when you play in India in festival matches, leagues, or outdoors. And when you arrive in an important competition with important teams".The coach said the significance of the win was that it came against Qatar, who arrived for the Games after a three-week training stint in Slovenia. "Qatar participated in the last two world championships and they also trained with the Japanese national team."On the big win serving as a confidence booster, he said, "Of course, it's good. articles.title: Red Sox's usually dependable bullpen implodes vs. Yankees in Game 1 rout
articles.summary: For the Boston Red Sox, it took all of three pitches to find out that a curious decision by manager Chad Tracy has them on the brink of elimination.
articles.body:
NEW YORK — One decision, in either direction, right or wrong, could mean the game or the series for postseason teams. For the Boston Red Sox , it took all of three pitches to find out that a curious decision by manager Chad Tracy has them on the brink of elimination.

After the New York Yankees ' 9-0 win in Game 1 of their AL wild-card series , Tracy was asked about his decision to pull starter Payton Tolle after 83 pitches. Tolle didn't show signs of fatigue when he was replaced by left-hander Erik Miller and went to the visitors' dugout, giving up five hits, one earned run, one walk, and four strikeouts.

Game 1 was Tracy's first postseason game as a manager, and before the matchup between the heated AL East rivals, he said he was most excited for the players because of the adversity they had faced this season, earning a playoff spot despite being 14 games under .500 in late June. He took over on an interim basis in April after Alex Cora was fired and led the team to a 77-58 record the rest of the way.

"I thought he threw the ball well. They did an effective job of grinding the count up as well. He had traffic. They put traffic on him. He was able to navigate his way through that. I think he competed extremely well for the time that he was out there and gave us what he could," Tracy said of Tolle.

"I think the number being up there in the mid-80s, still trying to get through five, probably higher than what you normally see with Payton, and to be expected in an environment like this. But I thought he competed his butt off."

2026 MLB playoffs open with thrilling wild-card series matchups

Miller, a 28-year-old left-hander, who was acquired from the San Francisco Giants on Aug. 3, had been outstanding in the regular season, striking out 74 batters in 51.1 innings in his 57 appearances, giving Boston much-needed middle relief down the stretch.

But Miller's first batter that he faced was designated hitter Ben Rice , and on his third pitch to the Yankees' leading home-run hitter, Rice deposited a 96-mph sinker that was right in the middle of the plate 423 feet to deep center field and Monument Park to extend the Yankees' lead to 2-0. Tolle had struck Rice out swinging in the third (the only time he was retired in the game) and gave up a double to him in the first.

That point of Tracy's decision could prove not to be the deciding factor, as the rest of his bullpen gave up seven more runs, including a grand slam to Rice, the 16th four-bagger in the Yankees' illustrious postseason history, in the bottom of the eighth inning to complete the scoring.

"I just think we were in a point where the way the game was going along, that if we could try to keep the game there, but also trying to keep guys short as we moved through it," Tracy said.

"Obviously, we had fallen down by four, and if we can try to keep guys short, stay in the game, and still have people online for tomorrow. But obviously the game was getting away from us at that point."

Rice finished with six RBIs, tying a team postseason record shared with four other players, and the Red Sox bullpen, which had the third-best ERA in baseball during the regular season at 3.27, couldn't get the outs that were needed at critical times. It's also too bad their opponents led MLB in that category at 3.15, as New York's relievers surrendered only a Trevor Story double in the top of the eighth in the final three innings.

Tracy's relievers were more than inefficient; the Yankees teed off on bad pitches and had great plate discipline. Tolle's night ended after he struck out four batters in his 4⅔ innings of work, and the Yankees, who struck out the sixth most of any team, whiffing 1,480 times in 2026, didn't strike out the rest of the game.

But no matter what the bullpen did, Boston's hitters could do nothing with Yankees starter Cam Schiltter, who struck out 10 in 6⅓ innings in 117 pitches of work and who, at one point, sent down 13 straight batters.

"Cam was obviously awfully good," Tracy said. "The fastball shapes are well-documented. He's throwing hard. He also had a good curveball today that you know it's there, but he used it a little bit more often. He landed it if he wanted to for strikes. He was able to get it beneath for a swing-and-miss. We weren't able to do much with him."

Compounding problems for the Red Sox was the injury to leadoff hitter Roman Anthony , who exited in the fifth inning after aggravating a wrist injury. Tracy says he is not sure of Anthony's availability for Game 2.

But the Red Sox are relying on Sonny Gray in Game 2 to help extend their season and give his battered bullpen some relief.

"I think we're very comfortable with all of our starters, the way that they've performed during the course of the season," Tracy said. "So having him out there tomorrow, anytime he's out there, we feel good about it. But having him out there tomorrow, obviously the season's on the line for us, and he can handle that."

articles.summary: Olivia Miles was on the wrong end of history after the Minnesota Lynx became the first No. 1 seed to get eliminated by the No. 8 seed in the playoffs. The Ly...
articles.body:
Olivia Miles was on the wrong end of history after the Minnesota Lynx became the first No. 1 seed to get eliminated by the No. 8 seed in the playoffs.

The Lynx bowed to the Liberty, 87-71, in Game 2 of their best-of-three first-round series at Barclays Center on Tuesday.

Miles, the newly minted Rookie of the Year, only had five points on 1-of-8 shooting. She also had two rebounds, one assist, one block, and one turnover. She only played 17 minutes.

She struggled in her first postseason , averaging just 8.0 points on 4-of-20 shooting, 1.0 assist, and 2.5 turnovers, which were way below her usual numbers.

The prolific guard was outplayed by Sabrina Ionescu in their marquee matchup.

The 23-year-old Miles looked lost against the Liberty, who capitalized on their experience, physicality, and size. She was left rueing her forgettable performance, as her electrifying campaign fizzled to a disappointing end.

She helped the Lynx to a 34-10 record, the most wins in franchise history. She held down the fort, along with Natasha Howard , Kayla McBride , and Courtney Williams , during the long absence of Napheesa Collier , who was recovering from ankle surgery before returning in July.

Miles, the No. 2 pick out of TCU, averaged 19.8 points, 4.7 rebounds, 6.0 assists, and 1.3 steals in the regular season. She was named to the All-Star Game.

The loss to the Liberty will sting for a while , but it should only motivate Miles to improve her game, make her body stronger, and come back with a vengeance in her sophomore year.

The Lynx have not won the championship since 2017.

articles.title: Kevin Danso and Sunderland: Why Pragmatism Can Be Progressive
articles.summary: Sunderland’s approach under Régis Le Bris may not always look ‘progressive’, but could Kevin Danso show why pragmatism is helping the Lads succeed?﻿
articles.body:
Terminology in football always tends to change. Closing-down became pressing, direct play evolved to vertical football, and having to defend is now referred to as suffering. When the elements of the game we all know are constantly redefined, you could be forgiven for forgetting that a knock-down from a long throw-in counts the same as a tap-in from 2 yards.

There is one particular adjective that is bandied around and continues to confuse me, because I don't know what a progressive manager is. According to the Oxford Dictionary, the word means " happening by degrees or favouring modern, forward-thinking reform ". Guardiola, Bielsa and Brighton 's Fabian Hürzeler have all had the term attached to them. But why?

Is Arteta's building of an incredibly physical squad to exploit set-pieces any more reformative than Guardiola bringing passing out from the back to English shores? How much added value has Vincent Kompany added to Bayern Munich after joining from a relegated Burnley ? Why is Antonio Conte seen as 'rigid' in his 3-4-3, yet Ruben Amorim and Xabi Alonso were seen as tactical pioneers?

Well, I'm not going to answer those questions for several reasons. One being that this is a Sunderland page, and another being that there's probably a book's worth of writing to be done there. But I do think there's a Wearside-centric conversation to be had here.

Régis Le Bris has not received enough credit for his work at Sunderland. The sound of his plaudits decays incredibly quickly the further away from the Stadium of Light you get. Whilst there was a vast quantity of money spent last summer, and figureheads like Granit Xhaka exponentially increased the quality of the squad, it was Le Bris who bonded that together.

Le Bris found the balance of his footballing principles, the foundations he had already laid in the Championship, and the humility against superior opposition to guide us to Europe last season. So why were we 4th favourites for relegation at the start of the season?

Well, before trying to answer that, there's another term worth introducing: pragmatic . Again, I'll look to Oxford, which defines the term as: "dealing with problems, decisions, or situations in a practical, sensible, and realistic way based on what actually works in real life, rather than following fixed theories, dogmas, or ideal rules".

Régis Le Bris is certainly seen as more of a pragmatic than a progressive figure in football, and should that be looked down upon as much as it feels?

I think Kevin Danso is the perfect vehicle to guide us through this conversation. The Austrian joined Spurs as competition to Cristian Romero and Micky van de Ven last February, with Ange Postecoglou stating, "Obviously we're a bit short at the back and have been for a while. He's experienced, a good one-on-one defender and new players give us energy."

Whilst not a glowing endorsement from the Australian, it was ultimately his fourth Tottenham Hotspur manager that saw Danso's exit, in Roberto De Zerbi. Romero also subsequently left the North London side this summer, but De Zerbi also saw the exit of promising youngster Luka Vušković, with replacements coming in the form of Jan Paul van Hecke , Marcos Senesi and Tosin Adarabioyo .

It is apparent that the keys to the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium have been given to the 47-year-old Italian, both with the quantity of money spent and in the places they have spent it. After a lengthy doping ban, Mykhailo Mudryk was reunited with the man he calls his " footballing father ". As already mentioned, Vušković departed, despite being named in the Bundesliga Team of the Season, and after aiding England to a World Cup semi-final, Djed Spence was allowed to leave for Italy .

Well, when you compare him to his apparent replacements in Senesi and van Hecke, it adds some context.

lbeit in fewer minutes than both Senesi and van Hecke, Danso's defensive numbers, for a poor Spurs side, last season dwarf both of his replacements. He was far more active in both aerial and ground duels, winning almost twice as many in the air as the Argentine did for Bournemouth . Danso was also a far more active defender, averaging almost 12 defensive contributions per 90.

Danso is clearly an adept and frequent defensive contributor to his sides; we've already seen that this season. But when you compare his work with the ball, you can begin to understand why he was allowed to leave North London.

van Hecke averaged around 60 passes per 90 last season, with Danso and Senesi averaging around 10 fewer. van Hecke and Senesi also managed over 20% of their passes to be line-breaking , meaning it was able to bypass a section of the opposition's defence, e.g. past a pressing front three or a midfield block. Danso only sat at around 13% of his passes for that metric. He also averaged fewer touches and accurate long balls than both of Spurs' new defenders.

De Zerbi has clearly made it clear that his defenders must be extremely comfortable on the ball, even if that means sacrificing both defensive actions and ability.

Of course, you can take these numbers with a pinch of salt. Both Bournemouth and Brighton fared better than Spurs last season. It's understandable that, as a central defender in a team that is fighting relegation, a simple shorter pass may be more favourable than a risky cross-field one.

Danso was never first-choice at Tottenham, but another thing Senesi and van Hecke had last season was the stability of playing under a single manager. It wouldn't have helped that he had to win favour with Thomas Frank, Igor Tudor and Roberto De Zerbi, even after the departure of the manager who brought him in.

Regardless, Danso's numbers show him as a centre-back who will frequently seek to break down or stop attacks, and at a relatively high success rate.

In his book ' How to Win the Premier League ', Ian Graham speaks of how it can be difficult to analyse the quality of defenders and uses Liam Ridgewell to convey this. At the end of the 2007/08 season, Ridgewell ranked amongst the best in Europe for his frequent number of blocks, clearances and last-ditch tackles. Graham goes on to mention that, without video analysis, it would've also been difficult to notice that he was also liable for a number of the chances Birmingham conceded that season.

Whilst he wasn't alone or a standout in that regard, it did provide context and an added dimension to what you would consider 'defensive responsibility' . The frequency of defensive actions doesn't indicate their quality or their cause. Danso is certainly not a calamity at the back, but it is worth considering.

So what does all this have to do with Sunderland? Well, the likelihood is that Danso will become a permanent member of the club next summer, and more pertinently, a significant fixture of our defence this season. But I think there's a few more ways you can look at this.

I don't think it's unfair to say Régis Le Bris has shown himself to be conservative in the Premier League so far; it's certainly not meant as an insult. His tactics have found ways to ensure the side have a solid, defensive foundation, whilst allowing the likes of Le Fée, Brobbey and Isidor to shine when the opportunity arises.

When I mentioned progressive managers before, I've recently grown to find Le Bris' use of Hume or Meunier really intelligent. Nordi Mukiele provides so much going forward as a right-back, and has the additional cover of those hybrid wingers/full-backs when Sunderland are out of possession. I think that is why Danso makes a lot of sense; he allows Mukiele to operate on the right and is athletic enough to cover the space left when he does roam upfield.

However, you'd like to think there would be a point where the metaphorical handbrake can be taken off. The Manchester City game certainly showed that we have the attacking quality and offensive movements to harm the best that England has to offer. I hope Le Bris does trust his side to play like this with two traditional wingers at points this season.

And that is why Danso is such a brilliant representation of where Sunderland are at. Many can consider prioritising a centre-back's defensive abilities somewhat archaic, but under Le Bris, it is pivotal that a solid base is there to allow our forwards to do their best work.

There may be a time when we seek more progression from deeper areas of the field, but what we've landed upon has brought us to European football. Whilst some may not consider our football sexy, and some may not think of Danso as a modern elite centre-back, the effectiveness of both cannot be questioned.

We're at a position where a move from one of the traditional 'big 6' to Sunderland for a peak-age player is not seen as a step down. It may even, and can perhaps even, provide a platform for players to shine and display their full arsenal of abilities. You'd hope that, as we grow with Le Bris, his confidence to play more expansively would grow with it.

We've seen glimpses in the Championship, and now in the Premier League, of how Le Bris can enable more offensive play. I'd argue if you want to measure it in the coming season, take a look at Kevin Danso.

articles.title: A’ja Wilson, Aces frazzled and frustrated in Fever loss. In Game 3, they must reclaim their identity
articles.summary: INDIANAPOLIS — Her night long since combusted, A’ja Wilson had her say one more time. This was after the shouting match with a heckler, and the boos, and the...
articles.body:
INDIANAPOLIS — Her night long since combusted, A'ja Wilson had her say one more time. This was after the shouting match with a heckler, and the boos, and the face she made coming off the court, and the expletive-laden explanation of her side. She was in a Gainbridge Fieldhouse hallway. The audience was her head coach, who was on the way to the room the Las Vegas Aces star had vacated after four questions.

Becky Hammon stopped, and Wilson continued her locomotive of thought about what happened during a Game 2 first-round playoff loss to the Indiana Fever on Tuesday. She said she didn't go at the heckler, but also maybe kind of did. But she wasn't going to allow some random person to point at her and say whatever he said. And then he backs off and sits down? No way this man says that to LeBron James, the four-time WNBA MVP declared. And then they let the guy back in his seat?

Many points, driven in like foundation piles. Wilson finished, turned to continue on, and a voice stopped her. A fan in a wheelchair found a marker for the autograph he'd requested. Wilson smiled and obliged.

Such was the whiplash of an evening when the defending champions were not themselves, in any useful way. As tightly wound as their emphatic Game 1 win was in Las Vegas , their 99-89 defeat in Game 2 in Gainbridge Fieldhouse left loose ends all over the place. Basically three quarters away from the next round, Las Vegas unspooled, alarmingly. Now it will have to fend off the end of the season, at the hands of a team trying to be the next version of the Aces.

Wilson was hardly the only Aces player to swerve out of character on the floor Tuesday. They're of course human. They're also the group that should be above and beyond the traps they fell into.

"Their urgency was a lot higher, the intensity was a lot higher," Wilson said. "Kind of had us on our heels, the same way we had them in Game 1. We'll be better. We'll adjust, and we'll come back with a better sense of urgency, effort and heart."

That was the basketball part. Defensive lapses and hurried offensive choices. That was hardly the end of it. One unfortunate event represented a scattered mindset behind everything.

Fourth quarter, four minutes and 10 seconds remaining. Wilson and Fever guard Sophie Cunningham bearhug as Wilson rolled off a screen. Cunningham hit the ground but caught the rap for the foul. Wilson walked away. A man in a baseline seating section stood up, took a step forward and pointed at the Aces star. "The foul's on you!" he shouted, according to another fan nearby who heard the exchange.

With that, Wilson removed her mouthpiece, left the court and walked toward the fan, admonishing him for pointing at her. Players and security personnel intervened. Wilson got hit with a technical foul for, evidently, leaving the floor. Plus side: Support staff for an Indiana Fever game is well trained in hell-breaks-loose protocols. Minus side: The unshakeable Las Vegas Aces seemed shook.

"I don't know if you guys know me, but I don't really get into the bulls—," Wilson said during her postgame news conference.

"I try to play my game, keep it pushing. But if I'm just walking, because I just got the foul, I'm chilling. And if I see a man come at me, taking steps towards me and pointing at me, I don't give a damn what you said, I don't give a damn how you said it, the tone – that is unacceptable. You don't step towards me. And point at me. I'm not for that s—. At all. Excuse my French, and God bless me. But that there is unacceptable. And how he gets back in the game because they said he didn't do anything – of course he didn't. And that's hard.

"And I apologized to my team because I got us a tech. But it's just certain things I'm just not going to allow anymore. Because it's just unacceptable."

Hammon, as one would expect for a coach trying to figure out what lifeline to throw her group, didn't see the instigating event. She did see the aftermath. She didn't really recognize it.

"I've never seen A'ja Wilson go like that," Hammon said. "So whatever was done, I can tell you she felt very disrespected in that moment. I can just speak to her — I've never seen her really react like that. Ever. So whatever it was doesn't have any place, I don't think, in an arena."

The unofficial litigation will continue for days, naturally. It is the second time this season the Aces have objected to something said by a fan at Gainbridge Fieldhouse, asking for that fan's removal. "Clearly lines get crossed," Hammon said, "and it seems to happen here." A Fever statement said security interviewed the fan and witnesses and determined there was no violation. The WNBA has no rule about players entering the stands, meanwhile, so apparently Wilson is under no threat of further examination and consequences.

But to hear Hammon describe her surprise at Wilson's reaction is to get the gist of the night. It may be that the Aces are fed up with fans in this city. It also may be that if the Aces were winning, and if they'd resembled anything close to the best version of themselves, then Wilson might have been oblivious to one bloviating fan and avoided the tripwire. These episodes usually don't occur in a vacuum.

This was not who Las Vegas expects to be, in any sense, and Indiana took advantage. The Fever have a Big Three, just like the Aces do. They're more callow, but they're ambitious. They're not there yet, but they have their sights on a legacy similar to the one Las Vegas has authored already. They're one win closer due to the model franchise splitting at the seams.

Before Game 2, while wearing fuzzy slippers with a smiley face on them, Wilson talked about bringing the proper energy and positive vibes on nights like these, so her teammates can follow. By the end, she and the Aces walked off the floor to a round of boos, and out of sight in the exit tunnel, Wilson stuck out her tongue and threw up two thumbs down to mock the crowd.

Neither she nor her teammates can be blamed for their frustration, or salty reactions to a salty sendoff. They do have to retake ownership of their identity by Game 3 at Michelob Ultra Arena.

Imagine the finger-pointing if they don't.

"We weren't ourselves tonight," Hammon confirmed afterwards. "I suspect we will look more like ourselves Thursday."

articles.title: Four thoughts from Week 4 in the American Conference
articles.summary: The Trace Johnson experiment needs to work at Tulane. Also, UAB has its best defense since joining the American.
articles.body:
Four weeks of American Conference play are in the books, and most teams are wrapping up non-conference play.

South Florida remains the only undefeated team at 4-0, while Tulsa had its first hiccup on the road at Arkansas. UAB picked up a signature Friday night conference victory over Navy, while ther other service academy, Army, survived a scare from Temple earlier that day. UTSA dropped 59 points on Colorado State and Tulane survived Southern Miss in a Will Hall revenge game.

It was an action-packed Week 4 in the American, and here are four thoughts from the week, ranging from the Big Easy to Boca Raton:

Tulane didn't replicate its non-conference success from 2025, and the Green Wave's prospects to return to the College Football Playoff took a significant hit in the month of September. However, they still operate with a blank slate in conference play, controlling their own destiny for a fifth-straight conference championship appearance.

How Trace Johnson performs will significantly dictate that. Tulane is set in the run game, even though starting running back Jamauri McClure sat out the entire month with a foot injury. The Green Wave are the only FBS team to showcase two different 200-yard rushers this year, as Jaylin Lucas attained 212 in the Week 2 win over South Alabama and Maurice Turner racked up 2022 in Week 4 against Southern Miss.

However, despite those prolific rushing performances, Tulane needed late-game heroics to stave off both the Jaguars and Golden Eagles in New Orleans. A stronger passing game, among other factors such as penalties, could have allowed Tulane to avoid these scares against Sun Belt competition at home. Tulane ranks 110th nationally in passing yards per game (186), operating with a 54.2 completion rate (10th-to-last in the FBS).

But late in the Southern Miss game, Tulane made a change which could define its season. Head coach Will Hall inserted true freshman Trace Johnson at quarterback. Johnson only finished 2-of-5 for 35 yards passing in a limited sample size. In all likelihood, he will be the starter going forward when Tulane returns to action Oct. 17 at Army. He would be the third different starter this year, following in the footsteps of Zeon Chriss-Gremillion and Kadin Semonza. Freshmen quarterbacks have worked out at Tulane before, and under Hall.

In Week 3 of the 2020 season, when Hall was offensive coordinator, the Green Wave thrust true freshman Michael Pratt into the Southern Miss game for a trial by fire. It worked out, and two years later, Pratt guided the program to its greatest win in history over USC in the Cotton Bowl. Time will tell if Johnson can write a similar story, but in order for Tulane to be successful this year, this gamble needs to pay dividends.

This is UAB's best defense since joining American

UAB is 1-0 in American play for the first time ever. The Blazers used to be the standard of Conference USA, qualifying for the conference championship game every year from 2018-20 and winning a pair of league titles. However, that success did not translate to the American, and UAB has spun its wheels in the basement of the conference since joining in 2023.

Friday night in Birmingham provided perhaps the first glimmer of hope since the Blazers joined the American. UAB had been defined by struggling defenses throughout its tenure in the conference, but the Week 4 win over Navy told a different story. The Blazers reasonably held a high-powered Navy rushing attack in check, limiting the Midshipmen to 4.2 yards per carry on 58 attempts and only allowing one run to gain more than 17 yards. UAB hasn't finished better than 120th nationally in run defense since joining the conference, but signs of improvement were evident in the American opener against Navy.

Navy also fumbled twice inside the UAB 40-yard line in the fourth quarter, and the Blazers capitalized on both miscues. UAB had the sixth-fewest turnovers created last year (9), and the team has already registered five takeaways in 2026. Longtime defensive coordinator Todd Grantham has proven UAB can take a step forward this year, and it has only allowed more than 21 points in one game so far.

There isn't much to say about Charlotte that hasn't already been said. The 2025 team went 1-11 and never finished with 11 points of an FBS opponent. The 2026 team has arguably been worse. The 49ers dropped their FCS matchup this year to The Citadel, which is 0-3 against its FCS peers with a 42-14 loss to Wofford and a 27-8 loss to Chattanooga.

In its Week 4 home game against Louisiana, Charlotte essentially did nothing. The 49ers completed 12 offensive possessions: six ended in punts (five were three-and-outs), three ended in fumbles, one ended in an interception, and the other a turnover on downs. Only one drive reached Louisiana territory — a 45-yard drive resulting in a fumble. Every other possession traveled 27 yards or fewer.

Charlotte finished with just 137 yards and finished 1-of-13 on third and fourth downs combined. The 49ers possessed the ball for roughly 19 minutes and lost the turnover battle 4-1. They avoided the shutout, however, as Louisiana got in its own way on a failed quarterback to running back exchange in the backfield, returning the fumble for a second quarter touchdown. Other than that, it's been the same story every game. Offensive struggles, defensive struggles, and not much improvement from week to week. The main question is, does Charlotte win a game in 2026? The conference slate features Memphis, North Texas, Temple, Tulane, UAB, East Carolina, Tulsa, and Navy. The current losing streak sits at 13.

Easton Messer had the coolest punt return of 2026

Easton Messer is arguably the top wide receiver in the American Conference. In his first season at Florida Atlantic, he finished third in the FBS with 104 receptions. He was one of three American receivers to exceed the 1,000-yard threshold and the only one to return to the league for 2026. Messer is currently second in the conference with 357 receiving yards so far this season, only trailing teammate Kelby Valsin by 29 yards.

While Messer had a quiet day on the offensive front in the Owls' 45-17 road domination of ULM, he still produced the greatest highlight of the night. The fifth-year senior receiver logged his first career punt return touchdown, and it was arguably the most impressive punt return of the season. Messer caught the ball off the bounce, ran nearly the length of the field horzontally from left to right, hit an effective spin move to escape the boundary, instantly juked tacklers from the front and back, and sprinted back toward the left side of the field for a 73-yard return. Watch this masterpiece.

The Owls, coming off a 4-8 season, are 3-1 for the first time since 2020. They currently ride their first three-game winning streak in six years as well, and they enter Week 5 as heavy favorites over FCS opponent Texas Southern.

articles.title: New video angle shows Indiana Fever were right not to eject fan after A’ja Wilson confrontation
articles.summary: A’ja Wilson was beside herself after seeing a fan try to heckle her, and tried to have him ejected. But new footage shows that would have been the wrong call...
articles.body:
A'ja Wilson was beside herself after seeing a fan try to heckle her, and tried to have him ejected. But new footage shows that would have been the wrong call.

A frustrated Wilson immediately rushed to the fan to confront him after she saw him heckle her and throw insults her way.

However, in a statement released after the game, the Indiana Fever confirmed that they reviewed the altercation and determined that the fan had not violated the code of conduct.

New footage shows fan just pointed and heckled A'ja Wilson, no lines were crossed

One fan on X shared footage that showed the incident between A'ja Wilson and the Indiana Fever fan sitting courtside.

While it may have been wildly disrespectful to A'ja Wilson, the footage confirms that the fan only pointed at her and didn't do anything that violated the WNBA's fan code of conduct.

After the game, the Indiana Fever confirmed in a statement that the fan's actions and words had been reviewed and that he had not been ejected, as he didn't violate the WNBA's fan code of conduct.

"Following a report of a comment directed toward a player, arena security spoke with the fan involved and witnesses.

"Security determined there was no violation of the Fan Code of Conduct, the fan was not removed from the arena. We consider the matter closed."

While there is no word on what words caught the ire of Wilson, even the Aces superstar did not allude to any foul or unacceptable language being used.

Rather, the point itself was considered the disrespectful gesture for the reigning league MVP, who did not hold back on the matter or the fan after the game.

The Fever have garnered a somewhat hostile reputation within the WNBA for housing an aggressive fanbase over the last few years.

Of course, this is far from the only courtside altercation between players and fans, as former NBA player Enes Kanter stirred up controversy when he attended an Indiana Fever game during the height of the league's controversy.

Hopefully, the fan incident is behind them and the Aces and Fever can continue to fight it out in Game 3 to see who gets one step closer to the WNBA Finals.

articles.title: Man United star training even on his off day, Michael Carrick needs him to hit the ground running
articles.summary: 3 It may be an international break, but one Manchester United star is not taking it easy as he looks to make an instant impact for his new club.After chasing...
articles.body:
It may be an international break, but one Manchester United star is not taking it easy as he looks to make an instant impact for his new club.

After chasing him for over a year, the Red Devils finally managed to land Carlos Baleba this summer, as the Cameroonian became the club's final signing of the window.

Michael Carrick wanted a midfield revamp , and he got it, but the former Brighton & Hove Albion star arrived injured.

Which meant that the head coach has had to wait to utilise his most costly summer signing. In fact, it is clear that it is the 22-year-old that United have missed the most so far this term.

Carrick badly needs Carlos Baleba in midfield

The 20-time English league champions have largely relied on Kobbie Mainoo and Youri Tielemans , and for all their quality on the ball, both are not as adept off it.

This has meant the leaky backline has not had the kind of protection it needs, with Carrick's team also struggling for intensity .

Carlos Baleba had made the matchday squad for the Fulham game but he did not come on in the end. All eyes are now on the Tottenham Hotspur game after the break to see if the Cameroon international finally earns his first United start.

According to The Manchester Evening News , the defensive midfielder has been busy attending individual training sessions as he seeks to hasten his recovery process.

Most players were granted holidays this past week, but the United No.20 was at it, and officials at United are confident that the Old Trafford side have signed a winner in the African star .

"United will need the Baleba of 2024/2025 to help turn this season around, but there is internal confidence in the highly skilled player they have signed. "Mark my words, he will be a success," was the message from a source close to the player when United's deal to sign him was confirmed.

"Baleba has settled in well at Carrington since arriving from Brighton . Sources say that although he was initially a tad shy, his bubbly, fun personality has come out as he has become more comfortable in his new surroundings.

"While the majority of United's players were given last week off, as is the norm for Premier League clubs, a few squad members reported to Carrington for individual sessions, and Baleba was among them."

Only time will tell if the £70 million recruit can save Carrick's job, but his dedication and hard work have already been recognised within the club.

articles.title: Gasly Forgave Colapinto: 'Everything Is Based on Respect'
articles.summary: The Frenchman accepted his teammate's apology after the Baku crash that knocked both of them out of the race. He acknowledged it was a hard blow in the fight...
articles.body:
PierreGasly has decided to turn the page. The French Alpine driver, who saw his race at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix end prematurely after a crash caused by his teammate, Franco Colapinto, has accepted the Argentine's apologies and appealed to mutual respect as the basis for maintaining a good relationshipwithin the team.

"Respect, you know, everything is about that at theend of the day. As long as there is respect, everything is possible," Gasly declared when asked if the camaraderie between both drivers will endure. Abrief but meaningful response that reflects the Frenchman's maturity inmanaging a delicate situation. Let's remember that the incident occurred on the first lap after the Safety Car restart in Baku, when Colapinto went wide on the braking at Turn 1, hit Gasly, and he, in turn, impacted Lando Norris's McLaren; as a consequence, the three drivers were out of the race due to the damage suffered.

In the heat of the moment after the race, Gasly had acknowledged his frustration: "I'm devastated, if you ask me, I'm not happy with what happened today, but I accept his apologies," the Frenchman had declared.

The blow was especially painful because Alpine was in anunbeatable position to score important points in the fight for fifth place inthe constructors' championship: "I felt very good in the car; thepace was almost as good as Lewis Hamilton's and the same as Lando's. I wasmaintaining a three-second difference with him until he locked up at turn 1, andafterward we had a 15-second advantage over Franco, who was coming behind. It'sstill hard to process what just happened," Gasly explained, reflectingthe magnitude of the lost opportunity.

The crash not only left both drivers without points but alsomeant a hard blow for Alpine in its fight with Racing Bulls for fifth place inthe constructors' championship. The French team has 68 points while the rivalteam accumulates 81, a difference that could have been smaller if Colapinto andGasly had completed the race in the positions they occupied. The five-place grid penalty for Colapinto, which will be applied at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, adds more pressure to the Argentine, who will have to come back from the rear on a demanding circuit .

Despite the disappointment, Gasly has opted for the path ofreconciliation. His message of mutual respect reminds us that in Formula 1,teammates must coexist and work together for the good of the project, even whencircumstances are adverse. Colapinto has acknowledged his mistake and asked for public apologies, and Gasly has accepted them with sportsmanship; the relationship between the two drivers, forged throughout the season, seems strong enough to overcome this episode.

Alpine now faces the season's final triple-header, needing to restore internal harmony and maximize its options in the fight for fifth place: The Malaysia race will be a new opportunity for Colapinto and Gasly to show they can work together and score points for the team. Respect, as Gasly says, is the basis of everything; without it, no project can prosper. With the right respect, even the most difficult moments can be overcome.

The French team trusts that this episode will be forgottenand that both drivers will refocus on what really matters: competing andscoring for Alpine.

articles.title: Sherdog Prospect Watch: Unbeaten Hazem Kayyali
articles.summary: Unbeaten Jordanian prospect Hazem Kayyali brings an unorthodox blend of striking and grappling into his PFL MENA 11 welterweight semifinal against the more e...
articles.body:
The upcoming Professional Fighters League event features a few unbeaten MENAfighters, including HazemKayyali . The 26-year-old Kayyali will co-headline PFL MENA 11 against BadreddineDiani in the semifinals of the 170-pound tournament.Representing Team Kombat in Amman, Jordan, Kayyali earned his spotafter defeating HassanShaaban via unanimous decision in July. His professional recordincludes three victories and two draws, but Kayyali also bringsextensive cage experience from his amateur career. His previousprofessional opponents have a combined record of 9-6-2, makingDiani (11-4, 4-1 PFL) the most experienced fighter Kayyali hasfaced as a professional. Kayyali is an unorthodox fighter who is comfortable in both thestriking and grappling phases of a fight, having already recorded asubmission and a technical knockout in his professional career. ABrazilian jiu-jitsu black belt, Kayyali keeps his guard low andoften employs a karate stance. He has an effective kicking game andfrequently uses oblique kicks. Kayyali also displays a variedstriking arsenal and creativity in his attacks. His lone TKOvictory was initiated by a suplex before he finished Sadok ElKefi with ground-and-pound 72 seconds into the fight.

Under the International Mixed Martial Arts Federation banner,Kayyali went on to win a gold medal at the 2021 MMA World Cup aftersubmitting EoinSheridan — who is also currently competing in the PFL and scored a "Knockout of the Year" contender in his most recentappearance — in the tournament final.

In his first and, so far, only PFL assignment, Kayyali showcasedhis fighting style and offered a closer look at his skill set. Inthe opening round, he kept the action on the feet and attackedShaaban with long-range kicks. In the second round, Kayyali tookthe fight to the canvas. While the Jordanian couldn't secure afinish, he controlled the action after locking in a tight bodytriangle. In the final frame, Kayyali was taken down with relativeease but managed to neutralize his opponent's offense until thereferee stood the fighters up. Kayyali spent much of the remainderof the round grinding against the cage and looking for anothertakedown, only to be reversed and finish the fight on his back. Thejudges ultimately awarded Kayyali the unanimous decision withscores of 29-28, 29-28 and 29-27, allowing him to advance in thetournament. The Denver Nuggets made a solid move to strengthen the roster around Nikola Jokic and Aaron Gordon when they brought Cam Whitmore into the fold . Whitmore's roster situation changed through several trades and transactions before he ultimately agreed to a two-way contract with Denver.

Now, Whitmore is already turning heads at training camp. During the Nuggets' first day of training camp, Gordon gave Whitmore a notable shoutout .

"Big Cam. Cam's a very good player. He's big, strong, he's talented, and he's going to be a good addition. I hope that he sticks," Gordon said.

Whitmore's NBA journey began with the Houston Rockets , who selected him with the 20th overall pick in the 2023 NBA Draft. During his rookie season in Houston, Whitmore averaged 12.3 points while playing just 18.7 minutes per game.

After spending his first two seasons with the Rockets, Whitmore joined the Washington Wizards . The 22-year-old averaged 9.2 points and 2.8 rebounds in 16.9 minutes over 21 regular-season appearances for Washington last season.

Unfortunately, Whitmore's time on the court was restricted after he was diagnosed with right shoulder deep vein thrombosis . The injury limited his ability to maintain a consistent presence during the season.

If Denver can get Whitmore fully healthy and comfortable within its system, he could give the Nuggets a major punch off the bench in the upcoming season, first on his current two-way contract and potentially a standard NBA deal before the playoffs roll around if everything goes as planned.

articles.title: 'Something deceptive': How Astros' bats were held in check by a variety of White Sox arms in Game 1
articles.summary: From Hagen Smith's low release point to Grant Taylor's high arm slot, the White Sox kept changing looks and Houston struggled to adjust as the Astros were pu...
articles.body:
In explaining his choice of young left-hander Hagen Smith to open Game 1 of the wild-card series against the Houston Astros , White Sox manager Will Venable said pregame that one factor was the "big hitter in the two-hole that we're concerned about."

That, of course, was Yordan Alvarez , the left-handed slugger and American League MVP frontrunner who mans the second spot in Houston 's lineup. Alvarez wields the potential to alter a game - and in this case, a best-of-three playoff series - with one swing.

Smith, in his three scoreless innings Tuesday for Chicago , faced Alvarez twice. Alvarez, a platoon-neutral slugger who posted an .825 OPS against lefties this season, grounded out twice, with the second ending the third inning with a runner on third base.

"I think the angle of his arm slot is something that's a little bit difficult," Alvarez said afterward, through an interpreter, of Smith, "and also we've never seen him before."

The first observation fell in with others the Astros offered after a 6-3 loss in Game 1 that left them on the brink of elimination . While the White Sox pounced on their pitchers early in a dueling bullpen game, the Astros struggled to generate offense against Chicago's series of arms.

Five pitchers for the White Sox combined to hold the Astros to six hits. None came in their seven at-bats with a runner in scoring position. Afterward, manager Joe Espada said he thought the variety of looks his hitters faced "was the difference in the game."

"They really gave us multiple different arms, different arm angles, they displayed different repertoires," Espada said. "I thought they did a nice job of just kind of mixing and matching and we just couldn't really get anything going."
